claim: Amazon EC2 basic monitoring publishes metrics at five-minute intervals; EC2 detailed monitoring publishes them at one-minute intervals.
question: At what interval does Amazon EC2 publish metrics to CloudWatch with basic monitoring and with detailed monitoring?

values.spoken: every five minutes with basic monitoring

qualifiers.condition: Detailed monitoring must be activated and incurs charges.

evidence.quote: Detailed monitoring options differ based on the services that offer it. For example, Amazon EC2 detailed monitoring provides more frequent metrics, published at one-minute intervals, instead of the five-minute intervals used in Amazon EC2 basic monitoring.

note: Neighbour fact ec2-auto-scaling-ec2-metrics-five-minute-default covers the Auto Scaling side. Other services publish at their own intervals.

claim: Many AWS services publish a default set of metrics to CloudWatch with basic monitoring at no charge, and basic monitoring is enabled automatically when you start using such a service.
question: Is basic monitoring in CloudWatch free, and do you have to turn it on?

evidence.quote: Many AWS services offer basic monitoring by publishing a default set of metrics to CloudWatch with no charge to customers. By default, when you start using one of these AWS services, basic monitoring is automatically enabled.

claim: Detailed monitoring is offered by only some services, it incurs charges, and you must choose to activate it for a service.
question: Is detailed monitoring available for every service, is it free, and is it on by default?

values.display: you must choose to activate it

evidence.quote: Detailed monitoring is offered by only some services. It also incurs charges. To use it for an AWS service, you must choose to activate it.

claim: Detailed monitoring has different names in different services: detailed monitoring in Amazon EC2, enhanced monitoring in AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and request metrics in Amazon S3.
question: What do Amazon EC2, AWS Elastic Beanstalk and Amazon S3 call their detailed monitoring?

evidence.quote: In different AWS services, detailed monitoring also has different names. For example, in Amazon EC2 it is called detailed monitoring, in AWS Elastic Beanstalk it is called enhanced monitoring, and in Amazon S3 it is called request metrics.

claim: Metrics from AWS services are standard resolution by default. A custom metric can be standard resolution or high resolution. A high-resolution metric is stored at a resolution of 1 second and can be retrieved with a period of 1, 5, 10 or 30 seconds, or any multiple of 60 seconds.
question: What resolution do metrics from AWS services have by default, and what periods can you use to read a high-resolution custom metric?

values.display: 1 second, 5 seconds, 10 seconds, 30 seconds, or any multiple of 60 seconds

qualifiers.condition: Standard resolution has one-minute granularity; high resolution is available for custom metrics.

evidence.quote: Metrics produced by AWS services are standard resolution by default. When you publish a custom metric, you can define it as either standard resolution or high resolution. When you publish a high-resolution metric, CloudWatch stores it with a resolution of 1 second, and you can read and retrieve it with a period of 1 second, 5 seconds, 10 seconds, 30 seconds, or any multiple of 60 seconds.

claim: For an alarm on a high-resolution metric you can set a high-resolution alarm with a period of 10 seconds or 30 seconds, or a regular alarm with a period that is any multiple of 60 seconds. High-resolution alarms cost more.
question: What are the shortest alarm periods CloudWatch allows on a high-resolution metric, and do they cost more?

values.display: a period of 10 seconds or 30 seconds

qualifiers.condition: The Alarm evaluation page of the same guide lists 10, 20 or 30 seconds; the Concepts and Publishing pages and the pricing page name 10 and 30 seconds.

evidence.quote: If you set an alarm on a high-resolution metric, you can specify a high-resolution alarm with a period of 10 seconds or 30 seconds, or you can set a regular alarm with a period of any multiple of 60 seconds. There is a higher charge for high-resolution alarms with a period of 10 or 30 seconds.

note: Source disagreement: alarm-evaluation.html says 'a period of 10 seconds, 20 seconds, or 30 seconds' and 'evaluated every 10 seconds'; cloudwatch_concepts, publishingMetrics and the pricing page say 10 or 30 seconds. Teach 10 and 30 seconds; do not teach 20 seconds.

claim: The minimum resolution CloudWatch supports is one-second data points (a high-resolution metric); metrics can also be stored at one-minute granularity.
question: What is the minimum resolution of data that CloudWatch receives and aggregates?

evidence.quote: The minimum resolution supported by CloudWatch is one-second data points, which is a high-resolution metric, or you can store metrics at one-minute granularity.

claim: If you do not mark a metric as high resolution with the StorageResolution field of PutMetricData, CloudWatch aggregates and stores it at one-minute resolution by default.
question: At what resolution does CloudWatch store a custom metric when StorageResolution is not set?

qualifiers.condition: High resolution is set per metric with the StorageResolution field.

evidence.quote: If you do not specify that a metric is high resolution, by setting the StorageResolution field in the PutMetricData API request, then by default CloudWatch will aggregate and store the metrics at one-minute resolution.

claim: Metrics cannot be deleted. They expire automatically after 15 months if no new data is published to them, and data points older than 15 months are dropped on a rolling basis. Metrics exist only in the Region where they are created.
question: Can you delete a CloudWatch metric, and when does a metric expire?

qualifiers.condition: The 15 months run from the last new data point.

evidence.quote: Metrics exist only in the Region in which they are created. Metrics cannot be deleted, but they automatically expire after 15 months if no new data is published to them. Data points older than 15 months expire on a rolling basis; as new data points come in, data older than 15 months is dropped.

claim: Data points published with a short period are aggregated for long-term storage. One-minute data stays at one-minute resolution for 15 days, is retrievable only at five-minute resolution after that, and only at one-hour resolution after 63 days.
question: How does CloudWatch roll up one-minute metric data as it ages?

evidence.quote: Data points that are initially published with a shorter period are aggregated together for long-term storage. For example, if you collect data using a period of 1 minute, the data remains available for 15 days with 1-minute resolution. After 15 days this data is still available, but is aggregated and is retrievable only with a resolution of 5 minutes. After 63 days, the data is further aggregated and is available with a resolution of 1 hour.

claim: CloudWatch stores metrics for terminated Amazon EC2 instances and deleted Elastic Load Balancers for 15 months.
question: Can you still see CloudWatch metrics of a terminated EC2 instance or a deleted Elastic Load Balancer, and for how long?

qualifiers.scope: metrics of terminated EC2 instances and deleted load balancers

evidence.quote: Yes. Amazon CloudWatch stores metrics for terminated Amazon EC2 instances or deleted Elastic Load Balancers for 15 months.

claim: Disabling monitoring for an Amazon EC2 instance does not lose its metrics data: you can still retrieve it within the retention schedules, although the console only searches metrics for two weeks after the last ingestion.
question: Do you lose metrics data if you disable monitoring for an EC2 instance?

values.display: You can always retrieve metrics data for any Amazon EC2 instance
limits the search of metrics to two weeks

evidence.quote: No. You can always retrieve metrics data for any Amazon EC2 instance based on the retention schedules described above. However, the CloudWatch console limits the search of metrics to two weeks after a metric is last ingested to ensure that the most up-to-date instances are shown in your namespace.

claim: CloudWatch does not support deleting metrics. Metrics expire according to the retention schedules.
question: Does CloudWatch let you delete metrics?

values.display: CloudWatch does not support metric deletion
Metrics expire based on the retention schedules

evidence.quote: CloudWatch does not support metric deletion. Metrics expire based on the retention schedules described above.

claim: You can assign up to 30 dimensions to a metric.
question: How many dimensions can one CloudWatch metric have?

qualifiers.condition: Classic CloudWatch metrics; OpenTelemetry metrics use labels instead.

evidence.quote: A dimension is a name/value pair that is part of the identity of a metric. You can assign up to 30 dimensions to a metric.

claim: OpenTelemetry metrics use labels instead of dimensions, and CloudWatch supports up to 150 labels per metric.
question: How many labels can an OpenTelemetry metric have in CloudWatch, compared with dimensions on a classic metric?

qualifiers.condition: Classic metrics support up to 30 dimensions.

evidence.quote: OpenTelemetry metrics use labels instead of dimensions. Labels serve a similar purpose but follow OpenTelemetry semantic conventions and support up to 150 labels per metric.

claim: A metric data point's time stamp can be up to two weeks in the past and up to two hours into the future.
question: How far in the past and in the future can a CloudWatch metric data point time stamp be?

values.display: up to two weeks in the past
up to two hours into the future

qualifiers.condition: If you provide no time stamp, CloudWatch uses the time the data point was received.

evidence.quote: The time stamp can be up to two weeks in the past and up to two hours into the future.

claim: A PutMetricData request is limited to 1 MB for HTTP POST requests, and to no more than 1000 different metrics. You can send the payload compressed with gzip.
question: What are the size and metric-count limits of one PutMetricData request?

qualifiers.condition: The metric count adds up MetricData and EntityMetricData.

evidence.quote: Each `PutMetricData` request is limited to 1 MB in size for HTTP POST requests. You can send a payload compressed by gzip. Each request is also limited to no more than 1000 different metrics (across both the `MetricData` and `EntityMetricData` properties).

claim: With the Values and Counts fields you can publish up to 150 values per metric in one PutMetricData request, and percentile statistics can then be retrieved.
question: How many values per metric can one PutMetricData request carry with the Values and Counts arrays?

qualifiers.condition: Applies when you use Values and Counts instead of single values.

evidence.quote: Using the `Values` and `Counts` method enables you to publish up to 150 values per metric with one `PutMetricData` request, and supports retrieving percentile statistics on this data.

claim: Every PutMetricData call for a custom metric is charged, so calling it more often on a high-resolution metric leads to higher charges.
question: Does publishing custom metrics more often cost more?

values.display: every PutMetricData call for a custom metric is charged

evidence.quote: Keep in mind that every `PutMetricData` call for a custom metric is charged, so calling `PutMetricData` more often on a high-resolution metric can lead to higher charges.
